title: Position at maximum positive velocity
question: For x = 6t² − t³ metres, find the position when velocity in the positive x direction is greatest.

steps.title: Differentiate position
steps.body: Positive-direction speed means the maximum positive velocity.

steps.title: Locate the maximum
steps.body: Set acceleration to zero. Velocity is a downward-opening parabola.

steps.title: Evaluate position
steps.body: Substitute the time into the original position function.

check: v(2)=12 m/s and d²v/dt² = −6 < 0. Speed magnitude later grows without bound in the negative direction; that is not the requested positive-direction maximum.

title: Acceleration of an exponential trajectory
question: For x = 15e^(−2t) m, find acceleration at t = 1 s.

steps.title: Differentiate once
steps.body: Velocity is negative as position decreases.

steps.title: Differentiate again
steps.body: Acceleration is positive.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: Use t = 1 s.

check: The printed choices incorrectly show m/s; acceleration must have units m/s².

title: Displacement for half the acceleration
question: Cart A (mass m) starts at rest with acceleration a and travels x in time t. Cart B (mass 4m) starts at rest with acceleration a/2. Find its distance in the same time.

steps.title: Write the first displacement
steps.body: With zero initial speed, displacement depends on acceleration and time.

steps.title: Use the second acceleration
steps.body: The given acceleration already accounts for any force or mass effects.

check: Doubling or quadrupling mass does not enter kinematics once acceleration is specified.

title: Magnitude of a vector combination
question: A = 12i − 16j and B = −24i + 10j. Find |C| for C = 2A − B.

steps.title: Combine components
steps.body: Subtract the entire vector B.

steps.title: Compute magnitude
steps.body: Use orthogonal components.

check: Both components contribute positively to the squared magnitude.

title: Vector needed for a vertical resultant
question: B + C points along +y and has magnitude |C|, where C = 3i + 4j. Find |B|.

steps.title: Find the required resultant
steps.body: C has magnitude 5, so the resultant is 5j.

steps.title: Subtract C
steps.body: Solve B = R − C.

title: Speed under constant planar acceleration
question: A particle starts at the origin with velocity 9.0j m/s and acceleration (2.0i − 4.0j) m/s². Find its speed when x = 15 m.

steps.title: Use horizontal position to find time
steps.body: The initial horizontal velocity is zero.

steps.title: Find both velocity components
steps.body: Acceleration changes each component independently.

steps.title: Take the magnitude
steps.body: Speed is not the algebraic sum of components.

check: The particle is moving downward at this time because vy < 0.

title: Building height from projectile range
question: A rock leaves a building at 12.2 m/s, 53° above horizontal, and lands 25 m from its base. Find the height; use g = 9.80 m/s².

steps.title: Find flight time
steps.body: Horizontal motion is uniform.

steps.title: Use vertical displacement
steps.body: Choose launch point as y = 0, so the ground is at −h.

steps.title: Calculate height
steps.body: Rearrange before substituting.

check: The flight time exceeds the return-to-launch-level time, consistent with landing below the roof.

title: Two positive charges from total charge and force
question: Two positive spheres have total charge 40 μC, are separated by 0.50 m, and repel with force 2.0 N. Find the smaller charge.

steps.title: Use Coulomb’s law
steps.body: Let the smaller charge be q.

steps.title: Solve the quadratic
steps.body: Select the smaller positive root.

check: The other charge is 38.56 μC; their sum is 40 μC and their Coulomb force is 2.0 N.

title: Force from two charges in a right triangle
question: Place Q₂ = +80 nC at (0,0), Q₁ = +60 nC at (0,3.0 mm), and q = +24 nC at (4.0 mm,0). Find the net force magnitude on q.

steps.title: Find distances and directions
steps.body: Both forces repel q. Q₁ produces a rightward and downward force.

steps.title: Calculate the two forces
steps.body: Use Coulomb’s law for each separation.

steps.title: Add components
steps.body: Take the magnitude only after adding vectors.

check: The resultant points about 11.8° below +x, consistent with repulsion from both positive charges.

title: Field at the midpoint offset from two unequal charges
question: Q = −6.0 nC is at (0,+0.60 m), q = +3.0 nC at (0,−0.60 m), and P at (0.80 m,0). Find the electric-field magnitude at P.

steps.title: Find equal source distances
steps.body: Each charge is 1.00 m from P.

steps.title: Resolve each field
steps.body: The negative charge pulls the field toward upper left; the positive charge gives upper right.

steps.title: Add and take magnitude
steps.body: The vertical components add while horizontal components oppose.

check: The result points up and left, toward the larger-magnitude negative charge.

title: Zero field outside two opposite charges
question: A −2.50 μC charge is at x = 0 and a +6.00 μC charge at x = 1.00 m. Find the finite point where E = 0.

steps.title: Choose the possible region
steps.body: Between opposite charges the fields point the same way. Cancellation must be left of the smaller charge.

steps.title: Equate magnitudes
steps.body: Let d > 0 be distance to the left of the negative charge.

steps.title: Solve the distance
steps.body: Take the positive square roots.

check: At this point the smaller negative charge is closer; the two fields have equal magnitude and opposite directions.

title: Electric field between thundercloud charge concentrations
question: An aircraft is at height 2000 m; +40.0 C is at 3000 m and −40.0 C at 1000 m. Treat the concentrations as point charges and find E at the aircraft.

steps.title: Identify directions
steps.body: The upper positive charge pushes downward; the lower negative charge attracts downward.

steps.title: Add equal magnitudes
steps.body: Each source is 1000 m away.

check: The two equal contributions add rather than cancel.

title: Axial field of a finite negative rod
question: A uniformly charged rod has length 0.140 m and total charge −22.0 μC. Find the field magnitude and direction on its axis 0.360 m from its center.

steps.title: Set the coordinate system
steps.body: Center the rod at the origin and evaluate at x = +0.360 m; λ = Q/L.

steps.title: Integrate axial contributions
steps.body: Every source-to-point displacement is along +x.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: The negative sign indicates a field toward the rod.

check: The result is slightly larger than k|Q|/x², and reduces to that point-charge result far away.

title: Field of a semi-infinite uniform line
question: A line with uniform linear density λ₀ extends along +x from x₀ > 0 to infinity. Find E at the origin.

steps.title: Write the vector element
steps.body: For positive density, each element produces a field toward −x.

steps.title: Integrate
steps.body: The far endpoint contributes zero.

check: Units are N/C; reverse the direction if λ₀ is negative.

title: Four axial fields of a charged ring
question: A uniformly charged ring has radius 0.100 m and charge +75.0 μC. Find the axial field at positive axial distances (a) 0.0100 m, (b) 0.0500 m, (c) 0.300 m, (d) 1.00 m.

steps.title: Use symmetry
steps.body: Transverse components cancel; axial components add.

steps.title: Evaluate near the center
steps.body: Keep all distances in metres.

steps.title: Evaluate farther away
steps.body: All four fields point away from the positively charged ring along +x.

check: The field initially increases, reaches a maximum at x=a/√2, and then decreases; a monotonic decrease from the center would be incorrect.

title: Field of a semi-infinite nonuniform line
question: A line extends from x₀ > 0 to infinity with linear charge density λ(x) = λ₀x₀/x. Find the electric field at the origin.

steps.title: Use the local density
steps.body: Charge in dx decreases with x.

steps.title: Integrate the vector field
steps.body: Positive charges produce a field toward −x.

steps.title: Apply limits
steps.body: The upper-limit term vanishes.

check: This is half the uniform-line result for the same starting density; negative λ₀ reverses direction.

title: Location and value of the ring-field maximum
question: Show where the magnitude of the axial field of a uniformly charged ring of radius a and charge Q is greatest, and derive its maximum value.

steps.title: Differentiate the positive-side magnitude
steps.body: Assume a > 0 and nonzero Q.

steps.title: Find the critical point
steps.body: The derivative changes from positive to negative.

steps.title: Substitute back
steps.body: There is an equal magnitude maximum on the negative side.

check: E vanishes at the center and tends to zero at infinity, confirming the interior extremum is the maximum.

title: Four axial fields of a uniformly charged disk
question: A disk has radius 0.350 m and surface density +7.90×10⁻³ C/m². Find the field at positive axial distances (a) 0.0500 m, (b) 0.100 m, (c) 0.500 m, (d) 2.00 m.

steps.title: Sum concentric rings
steps.body: A ring of radius r has charge σ2πr dr.

steps.title: Evaluate the nearer points
steps.body: Use the finite-disk expression, not the infinite-sheet approximation.

steps.title: Evaluate the farther points
steps.body: Each field points away from the disk on the selected positive side.

check: All values are below σ/(2ε₀)=4.46×10⁸ N/C and decrease with distance.

title: Far-field limit of a charged disk
question: Show that a uniformly charged disk of radius R and charge Q = σπR² acts like a point charge on its axis when x ≫ R.

steps.title: Rewrite the geometric factor
steps.body: Take x > 0.

steps.title: Apply the binomial approximation
steps.body: The small parameter is R²/x².

steps.title: Insert into the disk field
steps.body: Replace σπR² by Q.

check: The leading relative correction is −3R²/(4x²), so the approximation improves as distance increases.

title: Field at the center of a negative semicircular rod
question: A 0.140 m insulating rod is bent into the left half of a circle. It carries uniform charge −7.50 μC. Find the field at its center O.

steps.title: Convert arc length to radius
steps.body: The given length is the semicircular arc length, not its diameter.

steps.title: Use symmetry and integrate
steps.body: Vertical components cancel. Negative charge attracts toward the left semicircle.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.body: Take +x to the right.

check: The result points toward the negatively charged material and has zero vertical component.

title: Charge ratio from field-line counts
question: The diagram shows field lines leaving upper charge q₂, with some ending on lower charge q₁. Determine (a) q₁/q₂ and (b) both signs.

steps.title: Read arrow directions
steps.body: Lines leave q₂ and terminate on q₁, so q₂ is positive and q₁ is negative.

steps.title: Count lines
steps.body: Six lines terminate on q₁. Eighteen lines leave q₂: six terminate on q₁ and twelve extend outward.

steps.title: Restore the sign
steps.body: The charges have opposite signs.

check: The net positive charge explains why some lines extend to infinity.

title: Electron and proton speeds in a uniform field
question: An electron and proton start at rest in a uniform 520 N/C electric field. Find each speed after 48.0 ns.

steps.title: Apply electric force and Newton’s law
steps.body: The particles have equal charge magnitudes but very different masses.

steps.title: Calculate the electron speed
steps.body: Use me = 9.109×10⁻³¹ kg and t = 48.0×10⁻⁹ s.

steps.title: Calculate the proton speed
steps.body: Use mp = 1.673×10⁻²⁷ kg. The proton accelerates along E; the electron opposite E.

check: The speed ratio is mp/me ≈1836. Both speeds are sufficiently below c for the intended nonrelativistic model.

title: A proton brought to rest by an electric field
question: A proton initially moves along +x in E = −6.00×10⁵ i N/C and stops after 7.00 cm. Find (a) acceleration, (b) initial speed, and (c) stopping time.

steps.title: Calculate acceleration
steps.body: A positive proton accelerates in the field direction.

steps.title: Use the stopping distance
steps.body: Final speed is zero and displacement is +0.0700 m.

steps.title: Find stopping time
steps.body: Use final velocity = initial velocity + at.

check: Average speed during stopping is v₀/2; multiplying by the stopping time recovers 0.0700 m.

title: Flux through a triangular closed box
question: A triangular prism lies in a horizontal field E = 7.80×10⁴ N/C. Its vertical face is 10 cm high by 30 cm long; the sloped face makes 60° with the vertical in the end cross-section. Find outward flux through (a) vertical face, (b) slanted face, (c) the entire box.

steps.title: Calculate entering flux
steps.body: The vertical face normal points opposite the field.

steps.title: Calculate exiting flux
steps.body: The slanted face has the same projected area perpendicular to E. Alternatively its slant length is 0.10/cos60° = 0.20 m and its normal is 60° from E.

steps.title: Sum all faces
steps.body: The remaining faces have normals perpendicular to E, giving zero flux.

check: A uniform field has zero net flux through a closed surface containing no net charge.

title: Flux through coordinate-plane surfaces
question: A uniform field E = ai + bj intersects area A. Find flux if the surface lies in (a) yz, (b) xz, (c) xy. Specify the normal convention.

steps.title: Choose surface normals
steps.body: An open surface has two possible orientations. Choose +x, +y, and +z for the three cases.

steps.title: Use the dot product
steps.body: Only the component normal to each surface contributes.

steps.title: Evaluate each orientation
steps.body: The field has no z component.

check: Reversing the chosen normal reverses the sign of flux; the source does not specify normal orientations.

title: Net electric flux through a submarine
question: Charges +5.00 μC, −9.00 μC, +27.0 μC, and −84.0 μC lie inside a submarine. Find (a) net outward flux and (b) whether more field lines leave or enter.

steps.title: Sum enclosed charge
steps.body: Keep the algebraic signs.

steps.title: Apply Gauss’s law
steps.body: The detailed hull shape does not matter.

steps.title: Interpret the sign
steps.body: Negative outward flux means more lines enter than leave.

check: Only net enclosed charge controls total flux; the distribution of individual charges does not change this answer.

title: Flux of a nonuniform field through a rectangle
question: E = ay i + bz j + cx k, with constant a,b,c. Find flux through the xy rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ w and 0 ≤ y ≤ h.

steps.title: Choose the normal
steps.body: Use +z as the surface normal; reversing it changes the sign.

steps.title: Retain the normal component
steps.body: The x and y components do not cross the xy plane.

steps.title: Integrate
steps.body: The normal component varies linearly with x.

check: The average normal field is cw/2; multiplying by area wh gives the same flux.

title: Net flux and enclosed charge in a nonuniform field
question: A rectangular closed surface has height a = 0.400 m, depth b = 0.400 m and x-length c = 0.600 m. Its left face is at x = a and right face at x = a+c. E = (3.0+2.0x²)i N/C, with x in metres. Find net outward flux and enclosed charge.

steps.title: Identify the contributing faces
steps.body: Only faces normal to x carry flux; each has area ab = 0.160 m².

steps.title: Subtract incoming from outgoing flux
steps.body: Use the field value at each face, not the field at the center.

steps.title: Apply Gauss’s law
steps.body: The net flux is positive.

check: The constant 3.0 N/C term cancels. Integrating divergence 4x over the volume gives the same flux.

title: Field from perpendicular infinite sheets
question: Two infinite sheets are perpendicular, carrying +60 pC/m² and −80 pC/m². Find the field magnitude away from either sheet.

steps.title: Find each sheet’s field
steps.body: A single nonconducting infinite sheet produces |σ|/(2ε₀) on either side.

steps.title: Add perpendicular components
steps.body: The directions are orthogonal in every region.

check: Signs change component directions across sheets, but the magnitude remains the same.

title: Field inside a uniformly charged cylinder
question: A long nonconducting cylinder has radius 12 cm and uniform density +5.0 nC/m³. Find E at radius 5.0 cm.

steps.title: Choose an interior Gaussian cylinder
steps.body: Since r < R, only charge inside radius r is enclosed.

steps.title: Apply Gauss’s law
steps.body: Flux passes through the curved side only.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: Use r = 0.050 m.

check: Inside a uniformly charged cylinder the field grows linearly from zero at the axis.

title: Field outside a uniformly charged cylinder
question: Each 2.0 m length of a long cylinder of radius 4.0 mm contains +4.0 nC uniformly. Find E at radius 5.0 mm.

steps.title: Convert charge to charge per length
steps.body: The observation point is outside the cylinder.

steps.title: Apply exterior cylindrical Gauss law
steps.body: All charge within the Gaussian length is enclosed.

check: The result decreases as 1/r outside the cylinder and does not depend on its radius.

title: Field inside a cylinder with quadratic density
question: A long cylinder of radius 6.0 mm has volume density ρ(r) = αr² with α = 6.2 mC/m⁵. Find E at radius 2.0 mm.

steps.title: Integrate enclosed charge
steps.body: Use a dummy radius s; density is not constant across the Gaussian volume.

steps.title: Apply Gauss’s law
steps.body: The observation point is inside the cylinder.

check: The r³ dependence follows from enclosed charge proportional to r⁴ and flux area proportional to r.

title: Field within a charged cylindrical annulus
question: Uniform density +80 nC/m³ occupies a long cylindrical annulus between radii 1.0 mm and 3.0 mm. Find E at radius 2.0 mm.

steps.title: Enclose only occupied volume
steps.body: The central hollow region contributes no charge.

steps.title: Apply Gauss’s law
steps.body: The point lies within the charged annulus.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: Use ri = 0.001 m and r = 0.002 m.

check: The expression tends to zero as r approaches the inner radius.

title: Exterior field of two charged spherical shells
question: Concentric spherical surfaces have radii 1.0 cm and 3.0 cm, with uniform densities +40 pC/m² and +60 pC/m² respectively. Find E at r = 4.0 cm.

steps.title: Convert surface densities to charges
steps.body: Both complete shells are enclosed.

steps.title: Apply spherical Gauss law
steps.body: The exterior field equals that of the total charge at the center.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: Use metres and C/m².

check: Both positive shells contribute outward fields; surface area must be included before summing charges.

title: Exterior field of a charged conductor with a central charge
question: A +4.0 pC point charge lies at the center of a conducting spherical shell (inner radius 2.0 cm, outer radius 4.0 cm) whose net charge is +4.0 pC. Find E at r = 6.0 cm.

steps.title: Track induced charges
steps.body: The inner surface has −4.0 pC so the metal’s field vanishes. The outer surface then has +8.0 pC.

steps.title: Find total enclosed charge
steps.body: The external Gaussian sphere contains point charge plus shell net charge.

steps.title: Calculate the exterior field
steps.body: Use spherical symmetry.

check: Surface charges −4 pC and +8 pC sum to the specified +4 pC conductor charge.

title: Exterior field of a wire and conducting cylindrical shell
question: A long central wire has λw = −8.0 pC/m. A coaxial metallic shell (inner radius 1.0 cm, outer radius 2.0 cm) has net λshell = −4.0 pC/m. Find E at radius 3.0 cm.

steps.title: Add all enclosed charge per length
steps.body: The observation point is outside both wire and shell.

steps.title: Apply cylindrical Gauss law
steps.body: Use the magnitude for the requested field strength.

steps.title: Determine direction
steps.body: The enclosed charge is negative, so the field points toward the axis.

check: The induced inner-surface charge is +8 pC/m and outer-surface charge is −12 pC/m, preserving net shell charge −4 pC/m.

title: Induced charge density on a conductor’s inner surface
question: A +6.0 nC point charge lies at the center of a conducting spherical shell with inner radius 1.0 cm, outer radius 2.0 cm and net shell charge −4.0 nC. Find the inner-surface charge density.

steps.title: Use zero field in the metal
steps.body: A Gaussian surface within the conductor encloses zero net charge.

steps.title: Divide by the inner surface area
steps.body: The central charge gives spherical symmetry, so density is uniform.

check: The outer surface carries +2.0 nC, so −6.0 + 2.0 = −4.0 nC equals the specified shell net charge.

title: Accelerating a proton and an electron
question: Find the speed of (a) a proton accelerated from rest through 120 V and (b) an electron accelerated through the same potential-difference magnitude (also taking its initial speed as zero).

steps.title: Convert electrical energy to kinetic energy
steps.body: Acceleration increases kinetic energy by the charge magnitude times the potential-difference magnitude. The proton moves toward lower potential; the electron moves toward higher potential.

steps.title: Insert each particle mass
steps.body: Use e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, proton mass 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and electron mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

check: Both particles gain 120 eV. The lighter electron is faster by √(mp/me) ≈ 42.8; both speeds are nonrelativistic.

title: Potential and field from a linear function
question: V(x) = 10.0 − 7.00x volts for 0 ≤ x ≤ 6.00 m. Find (a) V and (b) the magnitude and direction of E at x = 0, 3.00 and 6.00 m.

steps.title: Evaluate the potential
steps.body: Substitute each coordinate in the given linear function.
steps.math: V(0)=10.0\ \mathrm V,\quad V(3)=-11.0\ \mathrm V,\quad V(6)=-32.0\ \mathrm V

steps.title: Differentiate
steps.body: Electric field is the negative spatial derivative. The constant slope gives the same field throughout the stated region.

answer: V=(10.0,-11.0,-32.0)\ \mathrm V;\qquad\mathbf E=7.00\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{V/m}\ \text{at all three points}
check: Potential decreases toward +x, so the field points +x. Endpoint values use the field within the stated region.

title: Symmetric charges: zero field, nonzero potential
question: Two +2.00 μC charges lie at x = −0.800 m and +0.800 m. A positive test charge q = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁸ C is at the origin. Find (a) its net force, (b) E at the origin and (c) V at the origin relative to infinity.

steps.title: Add the fields as vectors
steps.body: Equal positive charges at equal distances produce equal, opposite x-directed fields at the origin.

steps.title: Find the test-charge force
steps.body: The force is the test charge times the net external field.

steps.title: Add potentials as scalars
steps.body: Both source charges give positive potential; their potentials do not cancel.

check: A zero potential gradient at the symmetry point does not require the potential itself to be zero.

title: Recovering a point charge from E and V
question: At a point near a single charge, |E| = 500 V/m and V = −3.00 kV relative to infinity. Find (a) the distance from the charge and (b) its magnitude.

steps.title: Eliminate charge
steps.body: Divide the point-charge potential magnitude by field magnitude.

steps.title: Recover charge
steps.body: Use the potential equation. Negative potential means the source charge is negative.

check: Substitution into k|Q|/r² returns 500 V/m.

title: Where field and potential vanish
question: A charge +q is at x = 0 and a charge −2q is at x = 2.00 m. Find every finite x for which (a) E = 0 and (b) V = 0.

steps.title: Locate possible field cancellation
steps.body: Between the charges both fields point right. To the right of −2q its field is stronger. Cancellation is possible only at x < 0, outside the smaller charge.

steps.title: Solve the field equation in its valid region
steps.body: For x < 0, distances are −x and 2−x. Take the positive square root and solve.

steps.title: Solve the scalar potential equation
steps.body: Potentials cancel when the distance to −2q is twice the distance to +q. The absolute-value equation has one root between the charges and one to their left.

check: Neither charge location is allowed. Checking field directions removes the spurious positive root of the squared field equation.

title: Energy of a four-charge rectangle
question: At the corners of a rectangle of height a = 0.200 m and width b = 0.400 m are +q (upper left), −2q (upper right), +2q (lower left) and +3q (lower right), with q = 6.00 μC. Find the quasistatic assembly energy from infinity.

steps.title: Count all six distinct charge pairs
steps.body: There are two vertical pairs, two horizontal pairs and two diagonal pairs; count each once. Each diagonal has length D = √(a²+b²).

steps.title: Evaluate the sum
steps.body: Vertical terms are attractive overall; horizontal terms are repulsive overall; diagonal terms are attractive overall.

steps.title: Interpret the sign
steps.body: The external agent does negative quasistatic work; 3.96 J is released during assembly.

check: The formula contains exactly 4·3/2 = 6 pair interactions. A negative result represents released energy, not a negative energy requirement magnitude.

title: Electric field from a three-dimensional potential
question: V = 5x − 3x²y + 2yz² in SI units. Find Ex, Ey, Ez and |E| at P = (1, 0, −2) m.

steps.title: Take the negative gradient
steps.body: Differentiate with respect to one coordinate at a time, holding the other two fixed.

steps.title: Evaluate at P
steps.body: At x = 1, y = 0, z = −2, the x and y components are both −5 V/m and the z component vanishes.

steps.title: Find the magnitude
steps.body: Use the Euclidean norm of the field vector.

check: The z component is zero at P because y = 0, even though z is nonzero.

title: Potential difference along a charged ring axis
question: A ring of radius R carries uniform total charge Q. Find the potential difference between its center and a point on its axis a distance 2R away. State the subtraction order.

steps.title: Sum scalar contributions around the ring
steps.body: Every charge element is the same distance √(R²+z²) from an axial point.

steps.title: Evaluate both points
steps.body: At the center the source distance is R; at z = 2R it is √5 R.

steps.title: Specify the sign convention
steps.body: Define the difference as final axial point minus center. The reverse subtraction changes its sign.

check: For Q > 0, potential decreases away from the ring center along its axis, so this difference is negative.

title: Potential difference near an infinite line charge
question: The radial field of an infinite uniform line charge is E = λ/(2πε₀r). Derive V(r₂) − V(r₁).

steps.title: Integrate the field
steps.body: Choose a radial path; the potential difference is minus the field line integral.

steps.title: Evaluate the logarithm
steps.body: The ratio of radii is dimensionless.

steps.title: Choose a finite reference
steps.body: An infinite line charge cannot use a finite zero at infinity because the logarithm diverges. The finite-radius potential difference remains well-defined.

check: For positive λ and r₂ > r₁, the potential difference is negative, consistent with the outward electric field.

title: Parallel plates: field, charge and capacitance
question: Air-filled parallel plates have area 7.60 cm² and separation 1.80 mm, with 20.0 V applied. Find (a) field, (b) surface charge density, (c) capacitance and (d) charge on each plate. Neglect edge effects.

steps.title: Convert dimensions and find the field
steps.body: Area is 7.60 × 10⁻⁴ m² and separation is 1.80 × 10⁻³ m.

steps.title: Find surface charge density
steps.body: The air-filled field relation gives the magnitude on either plate.

steps.title: Find capacitance and plate charges
steps.body: Use parallel-plate capacitance and Q = CV.

check: σA agrees with CV. The field points from the positive plate toward the negative plate.

title: Charge sharing after switching
question: C₁ = 6.00 μF is charged from a 20.0 V battery by closing S₁ while S₂ is open. S₁ is opened, then S₂ connects initially uncharged C₂ = 3.00 μF in parallel. Find the initial charge on C₁ and final charge on each capacitor.

steps.title: Charge the first capacitor
steps.body: Initially only C₁ is connected across the battery.

steps.title: Conserve charge after disconnecting the battery
steps.body: Both capacitors share a final voltage. Total positive-plate charge remains 120 μC.

steps.title: Allocate the final charge
steps.body: Each final charge is its capacitance times the common voltage.

answer: Q_{1i}=120\ \mu\mathrm C;\quad Q_{1f}=80.0\ \mu\mathrm C;\quad Q_{2f}=40.0\ \mu\mathrm C
check: Final positive-plate charges sum to 120 μC; each negative plate has the opposite charge. Electrostatic energy is not conserved during charge redistribution.

title: Stored energy at two battery voltages
question: A 3.00 μF capacitor is connected to (a) a 12.0 V battery and (b) a 6.00 V battery. Find stored energy in each case.

steps.title: Use the voltage form of capacitor energy
steps.body: For a capacitor held at voltage V, U = CV²/2.

steps.title: Evaluate the lower voltage
steps.body: Halving the voltage reduces energy to one quarter.

title: Doubling separation at fixed charge
question: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery. By what fraction does its stored energy change when the plate separation doubles?

steps.title: Identify the conserved quantity
steps.body: Disconnection means plate charge remains fixed; the voltage is free to change.

steps.title: Use the fixed-charge energy expression
steps.body: At constant Q, energy is inversely proportional to capacitance.

check: Mechanical work is needed to pull the attracting plates apart; that work supplies the increased field energy.

title: Isolated capacitor immersed in water
question: An air capacitor has separation 1.50 cm and plate area 25.0 cm². It is charged to 250 V, disconnected, then fully immersed in insulating distilled water. Find (a) charge before/after, (b) final capacitance and voltage, and (c) energy change. The handout does not specify the dielectric constant κ; give κ-dependent results and an explicitly conditional numerical example for κ = 80.0.

steps.title: Calculate initial capacitance and charge
steps.body: Treat air as vacuum and neglect fringing. Disconnection conserves free plate charge.

steps.title: Insert dielectric at fixed charge
steps.body: A fully filling dielectric multiplies capacitance by κ; fixed charge means the voltage divides by κ.

steps.title: Compute energy change
steps.body: Use Q²/(2C) because the battery is disconnected.

steps.title: Illustrate with κ = 80.0
steps.body: These numerical values assume κ = 80.0; the symbolic result applies for the dielectric constant supplied by your course table.

check: The plates have opposite signs. For any κ > 1, fixed-charge energy decreases. Numerical water results require a specified κ; the source omits it.

title: Find an unknown capacitance by charge sharing
question: An isolated unknown capacitor is charged to 100 V, then connected in parallel to an uncharged 10.0 μF capacitor. Their final voltage is 30.0 V. Find the unknown capacitance.

steps.title: Conserve charge
steps.body: Initial charge on the unknown capacitor equals total final charge.

steps.title: Solve for capacitance
steps.body: Move the C terms to the same side.

check: Initial charge is 428.6 μC; final charges 128.6 μC and 300 μC sum to the same value.

title: Dielectric insertion with the battery connected
question: A parallel-plate capacitor, separation d, remains connected to a battery at ΔV₀ while a dielectric of thickness d and constant κ fills its gap. (a) Show U/U₀ = κ and explain the energy increase. (b) Find the change in charge.

steps.title: Identify the fixed voltage
steps.body: The battery holds voltage constant while the dielectric increases capacitance.

steps.title: Find the energy ratio
steps.body: Use CV²/2 for this fixed-voltage process.

steps.title: Find charge and explain the energy source
steps.body: The battery supplies additional charge and energy. During quasistatic insertion, half of the supplied energy increases stored field energy and the remainder can appear as mechanical work.

check: This is fixed voltage, not fixed charge. The battery is the energy source; inserting a dielectric does not create energy.

title: Reconnect charged capacitors with reversed polarity
question: C₁ = 6.00 μF and C₂ = 2.00 μF are charged in parallel across 250 V, disconnected, then connected positive-to-negative and negative-to-positive. Find the resulting charge on each capacitor.

steps.title: Compute initial charges
steps.body: Take the node containing the initially positive plate of C₁ as the positive reference node.

steps.title: Conserve signed node charge
steps.body: Because the connections reverse C₂, the charge on that node is the difference, not the sum.

steps.title: Recover each capacitor charge
steps.body: C₁ retains its original polarity. C₂ reverses polarity because its initially negative plate is on the final positive node.

check: Final charge on the reference node is 750 + 250 = 1000 μC, equal to the initial signed sum.

title: Energy in a capacitor network
question: In the diagram C₁ = 50 μF and C₂ = 30 μF form one parallel group; C₃ = 36 μF and C₄ = 12 μF form a second parallel group. The two groups are in series across V₀ = 30 V. Find the energy in C₃ and select the answer.

steps.title: Reduce each parallel group
steps.body: The common top conductor joins the two groups; the battery separates the bottom nodes, so the groups are in series.

steps.title: Find the right-group voltage
steps.body: Series groups have equal charge. The smaller group receives the larger voltage.
steps.math: C_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{80(48)}{80+48}=30\ \mu\mathrm F,\quad Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V_0=900\ \mu\mathrm C,\quad V_3=\frac{900}{48}=18.75\ \mathrm V

steps.title: Calculate C₃ energy
steps.body: C₃ shares the full right-group voltage.

check: The other group has 11.25 V, and the two group voltages sum to 30 V. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Voltage division in a series capacitor branch
question: C₁ = 5.0 μF is directly across a 24 V source. A parallel branch contains C₂ = 15 μF and C₃ = 30 μF in series. Find the voltage across C₂.

steps.title: Identify the branch voltage
steps.body: Both branches connect to the battery nodes, so the C₂–C₃ series pair has 24 V across it. C₁ does not change the ideal battery voltage.

steps.title: Find series charge and C₂ voltage
steps.body: Series capacitors carry equal charge magnitude.

check: V₃ = 8 V; V₂ + V₃ = 24 V. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Energy after same-polarity charge sharing
question: A 6.0 μF capacitor at 50 V and a 4.0 μF capacitor at 34 V are connected positive-to-positive and negative-to-negative. Find the final energy stored in the 6.0 μF capacitor.

steps.title: Conserve positive-node charge
steps.body: The charges add because the polarities match.

steps.title: Find equilibrium voltage
steps.body: Both capacitors share the same final voltage.

steps.title: Compute the requested capacitor energy
steps.body: Use only the 6.0 μF capacitance for its stored energy.

check: Final voltage lies between 34 V and 50 V; the printed key is B.

title: Unknown capacitor from two initial voltages
question: A 25 μF capacitor charged to 50 V is connected with matching polarity to an unknown capacitor C charged to 20 V. The final common voltage is 36 V. Find C.

steps.title: Write charge conservation
steps.body: Charge on the combined positive node is conserved.

steps.title: Solve for C
steps.body: The higher-voltage capacitor loses the charge gained by the lower-voltage capacitor.

check: Both sides give 1687.5 μC at the unrounded C. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Unknown initially uncharged capacitor
question: A 30 μF capacitor initially at 80 V is connected across an uncharged capacitor C. Their final voltage is 20 V. Find C.

steps.title: Conserve charge
steps.body: The initially uncharged capacitor contributes no initial node charge.

steps.title: Solve the total capacitance
steps.body: The fourfold decrease in voltage requires a fourfold increase in total capacitance.

check: Final charges are 600 μC and 1800 μC, totaling the original 2400 μC. Agrees with the key.

title: Pulling plates apart while connected to a battery
question: A parallel-plate capacitor initially has C₀, Q₀ and plate separation d at battery voltage V₀. Separation increases to 2d while the battery remains connected. Find the new capacitance and plate-charge magnitude.

steps.title: Use the new separation
steps.body: Capacitance is inversely proportional to plate spacing.

steps.title: Keep the voltage fixed
steps.body: Charge adjusts through the battery as capacitance changes.

check: Charge is not conserved on the capacitor because the battery stays connected. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Dielectric insertion after battery disconnection
question: A parallel-plate capacitor initially has C₀, Q₀ and V₀. It is disconnected from its battery and filled with a dielectric of constant 3. Find the final plate-charge magnitude and voltage.

steps.title: Keep the isolated charge fixed
steps.body: The disconnected plates cannot exchange free charge with a battery.

steps.title: Find the reduced voltage
steps.body: Voltage follows Q/C.

check: U_f = U₀/3 at fixed charge. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Charge passing through a light bulb
question: A bulb operates at 30 W and 120 V for 1.0 min. How much charge enters and leaves it?

steps.title: Find current from power
steps.body: Use the stated operating voltage and power.

steps.title: Convert minutes to seconds
steps.body: One minute is 60 s; charge is current times elapsed time.

check: Equal charge enters and leaves in steady state; the bulb does not consume charge. Agrees with the key.

title: Resistivity from wire dimensions
question: A 2.0 m wire of diameter 1.0 mm has resistance 0.45 Ω. Find the material resistivity.

steps.title: Calculate cross-sectional area
steps.body: Radius is half the diameter, 0.50 × 10⁻³ m.

steps.title: Rearrange the wire resistance formula
steps.body: R = ρL/A gives resistivity.

check: Using diameter as radius would incorrectly multiply the answer by four. Agrees with the key.

title: Resistance of a stretched wire
question: A conductor of length ℓ, radius r, resistivity ρ and resistance R is stretched to four times its original length. Find its new resistance, assuming unchanged resistivity and conserved material volume.

steps.title: Conserve wire volume
steps.body: Quadrupling length reduces the cross-sectional area to one quarter.

steps.title: Recalculate resistance
steps.body: Both the increased length and decreased area increase resistance.

check: The constant-volume, constant-resistivity assumptions are required for the textbook stretching model. Agrees with the printed key.

title: Voltage from an electron count
question: 5.0 × 10²¹ electrons pass through a 20 Ω resistor in 10 min. Find the potential-difference magnitude across it.

steps.title: Convert electron count to charge magnitude
steps.body: Multiply by the elementary charge; convert time to 600 s.

steps.title: Calculate current and voltage
steps.body: Use average current, then Ohm’s law.

check: The electron motion is opposite conventional current, but that does not change the requested voltage magnitude. Matches key C.

question: Iron and carbon each have resistance 10 Ω at 20 °C. Their temperature coefficients are +5.0 × 10⁻³ /°C and −0.50 × 10⁻³ /°C respectively. Use the linear model to find Rcarbon/Riron at −80 °C.

title: Power in the diagonal resistor

question: In the diagram the middle branch has a 20 Ω resistor below a 50 V source (+ at top), with 1.8 A upward. The left branch has a 30 V source (+ at top) and a bottom 10 Ω resistor. Find the current magnitude and direction through the 10 Ω resistor.

question: Travel from A to B through a 20 V source (− then +), a 20 Ω resistor carrying 1.5 A from A toward B, and a 12 V source (+ then −). Find VB − VA.

title: Brightness in a series-parallel bulb circuit
question: Three identical 100 W bulbs are connected to a 110 V source: bulb A is in series with parallel bulbs B and C. Which is brightest?

answer: \text{A is brightest; B and C are equally dimmer. (A)}

title: Magnetic acceleration of an electron
question: An electron has velocity 6.0 × 10⁶ m/s in +x. The field is B = (3.0, 1.5, 2.0) T. Find the magnetic-acceleration magnitude.

steps.title: Keep only perpendicular field components
steps.body: The x component is parallel to velocity and exerts no magnetic force.

steps.title: Find force and acceleration magnitudes
steps.body: Use the elementary-charge magnitude and electron mass.

steps.title: Check the force direction
steps.body: v × B has components −vBz in y and +vBy in z. Multiplication by the electron’s negative charge reverses both.

title: Infer field direction from an electron force
question: An electron moves in +x and experiences magnetic force in +z. Given Bx = 0, determine the magnetic-field direction.

steps.title: Account for negative charge
steps.body: F = q(v × B). For an electron, v × B must point opposite the force, toward −z.

steps.title: Apply the right-hand rule
steps.body: Since x × y = z, x × (−y) = −z. A z component of B would create an unwanted y force, so Bz = 0.

answer: \mathbf B\ \text{points in the negative y direction. (A)}
check: Multiplying the −z cross product by negative electron charge produces the specified +z force. Matches key A.

title: Solve a magnetic cross product for By
question: A +2.0 C charge moves with v = (2.0i + 4.0j + 6.0k) m/s and experiences F = (4.0i − 20j + 12k) N. Bx = 0. Find By.

steps.title: Expand the cross product
steps.body: Set B = (0, By, Bz) in F = q(v × B).

steps.title: Use the z component
steps.body: The z force directly isolates By.

steps.title: Verify the remaining components
steps.body: The y force gives Bz = 5.0 T, which also reproduces Fx.

title: Acceleration of a negatively charged particle
question: A 2.0 mg particle with charge −6.0 μC moves at 3.0 km/s in +x through B=(2i+3j+4k) mT. Find its acceleration.

steps.title: Convert to SI
steps.body: A milligram is 10⁻⁶ kg; retain the negative charge.

steps.title: Evaluate the cross product
steps.body: The x component of the field is parallel to the velocity and contributes no force.
steps.math: \mathbf v\times\mathbf B=3000\mathbf i\times(0.002\mathbf i+0.003\mathbf j+0.004\mathbf k)=-12\mathbf j+9\mathbf k

steps.title: Apply Newton’s law
steps.body: Multiplication by the negative charge reverses the cross-product direction.
steps.math: \mathbf a=\frac q m(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)=36\mathbf j-27\mathbf k\;\mathrm{m/s^2}

check: Acceleration is perpendicular to velocity and field. Matches key (a).

title: Net force on an L-shaped wire
question: A 25 A current flows from x=−2 m to 0, then y=0 to 3 m, in B=40 mT in +z. Find the force magnitude.

steps.title: Use endpoint displacement
steps.body: For a uniform field, the integral of dℓ equals end minus start.

steps.title: Add perpendicular force components
steps.body: Use i×k=−j and j×k=i.
steps.math: \mathbf F=I\Delta\mathbf r\times\mathbf B=25(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\times0.040\mathbf k=3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j\;\mathrm N

steps.title: Take the magnitude
steps.body: Combine components by Pythagoras.

check: The two segments separately produce −2j N and +3i N. Matches key (d).

title: Force on an inverted U-shaped wire
question: A wire rises a distance L, runs 2L in +x, then descends L. Current follows this path; uniform B points +y. Find the net magnetic force.

steps.title: Separate the three segments
steps.body: The two vertical legs are parallel or antiparallel to B, so each has zero magnetic force.

steps.title: Find the horizontal force
steps.body: The top segment carries current in +x, so i×j=k.

check: The endpoint displacement is 2L i, which gives the same net force. Matches key (b).

title: Torque on an 80-turn loop
question: An 80-turn rectangular loop has a=0.40 m, b=0.30 m and I=8.0 A. B=40 mT in +x. Its plane makes θ=30° with +x as shown. Find the torque magnitude about y.

steps.title: Identify the angle to the normal
steps.body: The torque formula uses the normal-to-field angle, 90°−θ, rather than the angle to the plane.

title: Current required for loop torque
question: A single-turn square loop is 50 cm on a side. A 70 mT field makes 40° with the loop plane. What current gives a torque of 1.0 N·m about the specified central axis?

title: Helix pitch and entry angle
question: A proton enters a 0.50 T field along +x with speed 60 km/s. Its helix pitch is 5.0 mm. Find the angle between its velocity and B.

steps.title: Find the cyclotron period

title: Classify a charged particle’s trajectory
question: A particle has m=3.0 μg and q=5.0 μC. In B=60j mT its initial velocity is (30j−40k) m/s. Determine the subsequent trajectory.

steps.title: Resolve the velocity
steps.body: Both a parallel and a perpendicular component are present, so the path is helical. Convert μg to 10⁻⁹ kg.

steps.body: Only the perpendicular speed enters the radius.

steps.title: Find the pitch
steps.body: The particle advances along +y during each turn.

title: Distance travelled in circular motion
question: A proton follows a circular path of radius 2.0 mm in B=0.25 T. Find its total distance in 1.0 s, using m=1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg and q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.

steps.title: Balance radial force
steps.body: Magnetic force supplies centripetal acceleration.

steps.title: Use constant speed
steps.body: Magnetism changes direction without changing speed; distance is speed times time.

check: Distance counts every revolution; it is not the final displacement. Matches key (d).

title: Electron cyclotron period
question: An electron moves in a circle of radius 15 cm in a 3.0 G uniform field. Find the period.

steps.title: Convert gauss to tesla
steps.body: Use 1 G=10⁻⁴ T.

steps.title: Eliminate the radius
steps.body: Combining T=2πr/v with r=mv/(|q|B) makes the period independent of radius.

title: Proton orbit after acceleration
question: A proton accelerates from rest through 2.5 kV, then enters B=0.60 T perpendicularly. Find its circular-path radius.

steps.title: Convert electric energy to kinetic energy
steps.body: The gain in kinetic energy is eΔV.

steps.title: Find the magnetic radius
steps.body: Substitute the speed into the radial-force result.

title: Field for a proton velocity selector
question: A velocity selector must transmit 2.0 keV protons with E=80 kV/m. Find B.

steps.title: Find proton speed

steps.body: Arrange crossed electric and magnetic forces in opposite directions.

title: Perpendicular fields of two long wires
question: A 30 A long wire lies along x. A 40 A long wire perpendicular to xy passes through (0,4,0) m. Find the magnetic-field magnitude at (0,2,0) m.

question: For I=20 A, three x-parallel wires carry 4I in +x at y=2 m, 3I in −x at y=−1 m, and I in +x at y=−3 m. Find B at the origin.

title: Field from concentric circular arcs
question: The shown wire has a clockwise quarter-circle of radius a=2.0 cm and a clockwise three-quarter-circle of radius b=4.0 cm, joined by radial segments. I=2.0 A. Find B at their common center P.

title: Voltage at the midpoint of a rotating rod
question: A rod of total length L=0.40 m pivots at its left end P with angular speed +2.0 rad/s (counterclockwise). B=0.20 T into the page. A is its midpoint, L/2 from P. Find VA−VP.

steps.title: Determine magnetic-force direction
steps.body: At the shown instant the rod points right and moves upward. The magnetic force on positive charges is inward toward P, making P higher in potential.

steps.title: Integrate over the requested part of the rod
steps.body: Local speed is ωr. Stop at A=L/2, not at the free end.
steps.math: V_A-V_P=\int_0^{L/2}(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\int_0^{L/2}\omega Br\,dr=-\frac{B\omega L^2}{8}

steps.title: Insert values

check: The free-end voltage would be −32 mV; midpoint labeling is essential. Matches key (c).

title: Ways to induce a coil current
question: Can a coil current be induced by (a) moving a magnet through it, (b) moving the coil toward a magnet, or (c) holding it near another coil whose current is increasing?

steps.title: Apply the flux-change criterion
steps.body: An induced emf exists when flux linkage changes; a closed conducting coil can then carry current.

steps.title: Check all three mechanisms
steps.body: Moving either the magnet or the coil changes their relative geometry and flux. Changing current in the nearby coil changes its field and therefore the first coil’s flux.

check: Motion is sufficient in (a) and (b), but changing field alone suffices in (c). Matches key (d).

title: Lenz’s law for a falling magnet
question: A bar magnet falls through a horizontal conducting loop, north pole downward. Viewed from above the loop, in what sequence does the induced current circulate?

steps.title: Analyze approach
steps.body: The approaching north pole increases downward magnetic flux. To oppose that increase, the loop produces an upward field: counterclockwise current viewed from above.

steps.title: Analyze departure
steps.body: After the magnet passes, downward flux decreases. The loop reinforces downward flux to oppose its decrease: clockwise current viewed from above.

check: The induced magnetic force opposes the magnet’s motion in both stages. The viewing direction is explicitly from above. Matches key (d).
